record.paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
record.context_brief: Uniqueness and divergence for the (2^ν+1)n+(2^ν−1) family
record.original_question: For every integer ν≥3, define T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=((2^ν+1)n+(2^ν−1))/2 when n is odd. Is the only cycle the trivial cycle Ω(1)=(1→2^ν→2^{ν−1}→…→2→1), so that C(2^ν+1,2^ν−1)={Ω(1)}, and do the positive integers decompose as N=G(1)∪G(∞) with a nonempty divergent set G(∞)?

evidence.quote: For the choice of the parameters a = 2ν + 1 and b = 2ν − 1 for ν ≥ 1. The corresponding map T is given by T (n) = { n/ 2 if n is even , ((2ν + 1)n + (2ν − 1))/ 2 if n is odd .

Conjecture 5.2. Let ν ≥ 3 and let the parameters a = 2ν + 1 and b = 2ν − 1, then the set C(a, b ) contains exactly one cycle. We have C(a, b ) = { Ω(1)} and N = G(1) ∪ G(∞ ), with G(∞ ) ̸= ∅ and the trivial cycle, of length ν + 1, is Ω(1) = (1 → 2ν → 2ν − 1 → . . . → 2 → 1).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $\nu\ge 3$ and define a map $T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by
\[
T(n)=\begin{cases} n/2, & n\text{ even},\\[2pt] \dfrac{(2^{\nu}+1)\,n+(2^{\nu}-1)}{2}, & n\text{ odd}. \end{cases}
\]
(Note that when $n$ is odd, $(2^{\nu}+1)n+(2^{\nu}-1)$ is even, so $T(n)\in\mathbb{N}$.) For a positive integer $n$, the orbit of $n$ is the sequence $n,T(n),T^2(n),\ldots$ A cycle of $T$ is a finite tuple $(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_L)$ of distinct positive integers with $T(n_i)=n_{i+1}$ for $1\le i<L$ and $T(n_L)=n_1$. Let $C(2^{\nu}+1,2^{\nu}-1)$ denote the set of all cycles of $T$. Let
\[
\Omega(1)=(1\to 2^{\nu}\to 2^{\nu-1}\to\cdots\to 2\to 1),
\]
the cycle of length $\nu+1$ obtained by iterating $T$ starting from $1$. Define
\[
G(1)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \text{the orbit of }n\text{ under }T\text{ eventually enters }\Omega(1)\},
\]
\[
G(\infty)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \text{the orbit of }n\text{ under }T\text{ is unbounded}\}.
\]

Prove or disprove the following for every $\nu\ge 3$:
(a) $C(2^{\nu}+1,2^{\nu}-1)=\{\Omega(1)\}$, i.e., $\Omega(1)$ is the unique cycle of $T$;
(b) $\mathbb{N}=G(1)\cup G(\infty)$ (every positive integer either eventually enters $\Omega(1)$ or has an unbounded orbit);
(c) $G(\infty)\neq\emptyset$ (there exists at least one positive integer with unbounded orbit).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as Conjecture 5.2 of a 2021 preprint on a generalized Syracuse problem. As a generalization of the Collatz/Syracuse-type dynamical conjectures (including the existence of divergent orbits, which is unknown even in much-studied cases), no proof or disproof is known; the question appears to remain open.
